Cow's Milk Protein Allergy (CMPA) is an immunologically mediated adverse reaction to bovine milk proteins (primarily casein fractions alpha-s1, alpha-s2, beta, kappa-casein and whey proteins beta-lactoglobulin and alpha-lactalbumin).
It can be IgE-mediated (immediate urticaria, angioedema, wheezing, anaphylaxis) or non-IgE-mediated (delayed proctocolitis with bloody stools, vomiting, severe eczema, failure to thrive).
Cow's Milk Protein Allergy is distinct from Lactose Intolerance.

Lactose intolerance is a non-immune enzyme deficiency (reduced intestinal mucosal lactase activity) causing osmotic diarrhea, abdominal bloating, and flatulence without systemic allergic manifestations.
CMPA requires complete elimination of milk proteins, whereas lactose intolerance allows dairy proteins with lactase enzyme replacement or fermented low-lactose dairy.

Lactose intolerance in children commonly occurs as a transient secondary lactase deficiency following acute viral gastroenteritis (such as rotavirus infection), where mucosal brush border enterocytes are temporarily denuded.

Managing secondary lactose intolerance involves continuing breastfeeding, offering curd (which contains endogenous bacterial beta-galactosidase), or temporary low-lactose feeding during mucosal recovery.

Egg allergy is one of the most common pediatric IgE-mediated food allergies, primarily driven by egg white proteins: ovomucoid (Gal d 1, heat-stable), ovalbumin (Gal d 2, heat-labile), ovotransferrin (Gal d 3), and lysozyme (Gal d 4).

Many children with egg allergy can safely tolerate extensively baked egg matrices (such as in thoroughly baked muffins or cakes), where high temperatures and wheat matrix interaction denature heat-labile ovalbumin proteins.
Peanut allergy is an IgE-mediated immune hypersensitivity directed against peanut seed storage proteins (Ara h 1, Ara h 2, Ara h 3 cupins/conglutins, and Ara h 6).
Peanut allergens are potent triggers of acute systemic anaphylaxis in sensitized children, requiring strict allergen avoidance and prescription of an emergency epinephrine auto-injector.

Early introduction guidelines (such as the LEAP trial recommendations) suggest that in infants with severe eczema or egg allergy, age-appropriate peanut forms (smooth peanut butter puree diluted in warm water or breast milk) introduced between 4 and 6 months under clinical guidance can significantly reduce peanut allergy development.
While some children may have co-sensitization, having a peanut allergy does not automatically mandate tree nut avoidance unless confirmed by clinical allergy testing.
Soy allergy involves IgE-mediated or non-IgE-mediated immune reactions against storage globulins Gly m 5 (beta-conglycinin) and Gly m 6 (glycinin).

Wheat-related disorders encompass three distinct conditions: IgE-mediated wheat allergy (acute urticaria, anaphylaxis, or baker's asthma), Celiac Disease (autoimmune enteropathy triggered by gluten prolamins in genetically predisposed individuals carrying HLA-DQ2/DQ8), and Non-Celiac Gluten Sensitivity (NCGS).

Celiac Disease is an autoimmune disease where dietary gluten (gliadin in wheat, secalin in rye, hordein in barley) triggers T-cell-mediated mucosal inflammation in the small intestine, leading to crypt hyperplasia and villous atrophy.
The only proven treatment for Celiac Disease is a strict, lifelong Gluten-Free Diet (GFD).
Cross-contamination with gluten in the home kitchen must be rigorously prevented for children with Celiac Disease.
Fish allergy is driven by parvalbumin (beta-parvalbumin), a calcium-binding sarcoplasmic protein that is heat-stable and resistant to digestive enzymes.

Weight-for-Age (WFA) is a composite anthropometric index reflecting both past linear growth and current body mass.

While exclusive breastfeeding provides the gold standard of infant nutrition, human breast milk naturally contains modest concentrations of vitamin D (typically 25 to 50 IU per liter), which is insufficient to prevent deficiency in infants with limited direct sun exposure.
Pediatric vitamin A deficiency manifests along a spectrum of ocular pathology termed xerophthalmia.

Early functional impairment presents as night blindness (nyctalopia), progressing to conjunctival xerosis, Bitot's spots (foamy keratinized plaques on the bulbar conjunctiva), corneal xerosis, and irreversible keratomalacia leading to corneal ulceration and blindness.

Pediatric vitamin B12 deficiency leads to megaloblastic anemia characterized by enlarged erythroblasts (megaloblasts), macrocytic red blood cells, hypersegmented neutrophils, and bone marrow ineffective erythropoiesis.
Neurological manifestations of B12 deficiency in infants and children can occur even in the absence of overt anemia.
Maternal screening and lactation supplementation protect infant neurodevelopment.
Pediatric folate deficiency impairs DNA synthesis during erythropoiesis, resulting in megaloblastic anemia indistinguishable on peripheral blood smear from vitamin B12 deficiency.

Pediatric zinc deficiency is characterized by linear growth retardation (stunting), impaired cellular immunity (lymphopenia and increased infection susceptibility), poor wound healing, hypogeusia (blunted taste sensation leading to appetite loss), diarrhea susceptibility, and in severe cases, acrodermatitis enteropathica-like periorificial skin lesions.

WHO and UNICEF guidelines recommend zinc supplementation (20 mg/day for children >6 months, 10 mg/day for infants <6 months, for 10–14 days) during and after acute diarrhea to restore mucosal enterocyte integrity, reduce stool frequency, and prevent recurrent episodes over subsequent months.
Iodine deficiency is the single greatest preventable cause of intellectual disability and brain damage worldwide.
Universal Salt Iodization (USI) is the primary public health strategy for preventing Iodine Deficiency Disorders (IDD) in India.

Pediatric vitamin C deficiency causes scurvy, characterized by defective vascular basement membrane collagen resulting in capillary fragility, bleeding gums, periosteal subperiosteal hemorrhages causing pseudoparalysis of limbs, follicular hyperkeratosis with corkscrew hairs, impaired wound healing, and irritability.
Pediatric hypomagnesemia can result from chronic diarrheal malabsorption or severe malnutrition.

Growth faltering is defined as a downward crossing of two or more major percentile channels on standard growth charts or a sustained absence of weight gain over 2 to 3 consecutive monthly measurements in infants.

Pediatric undernutrition encompasses a continuum of nutritional inadequacies categorized into stunting (low height-for-age, reflecting chronic long-term undernutrition), wasting (low weight-for-height, reflecting acute rapid weight loss), and underweight (composite low weight-for-age).

Protein-Energy Malnutrition (PEM) presents classically in two severe clinical syndromes: Marasmus (caused by severe caloric and protein starvation resulting in extreme generalized muscular wasting, loss of subcutaneous adipose tissue, and an 'old-man' facies) and Kwashiorkor (caused by inadequate protein intake in the presence of carbohydrates, leading to hypoalbuminemic bilateral pitting edema, hepatomegaly, and 'flaky-paint' dermatosis).
Children with SAM and medical complications require specialized inpatient stabilization, while uncomplicated SAM can be managed in community settings with Ready-to-Use Therapeutic Foods (RUTF).

Childhood overweight and obesity are characterized by abnormal or excessive adiposity that impairs physical and metabolic health.

Childhood obesity is driven by complex interactions between genetic predisposition and obesogenic environments featuring hyper-palatable ultra-processed foods (UPFs), sugar-sweetened beverages (SSBs), high refined starches, and increased sedentary screen time with reduced active outdoor play.

Acanthosis nigricans (velvety hyperpigmentation in skin folds such as the posterior neck and axillae) is a physical clinical sign of underlying hyperinsulinemia and insulin resistance in children with obesity.
Pediatric anemia in India is a major public health challenge, with National Family Health Survey (NFHS-5) data indicating over 67% prevalence among children aged 6 to 59 months.
Iron Deficiency Anemia (IDA) directly impairs neurocognitive functioning in young children.
Distinguishing nutritional iron deficiency anemia from hemoglobinopathies (such as Beta-Thalassemia Minor/Trait) is vital before initiating high-dose iron therapy.
In Thalassemia trait, red blood cell count is elevated relative to mild microcytic anemia with normal or high serum ferritin, and HbA2 exceeds 3.
Anemia Mukt Bharat (AMB) is the Indian national strategy utilizing the 6x6x6 framework to reduce anemia.

For children aged 5 to 9 years, Anemia Mukt Bharat provides weekly prophylactic IFA tablets containing 45 mg of elemental iron and 400 mcg of folic acid, while adolescents (10–19 years) receive weekly blue IFA tablets containing 60 mg of elemental iron and 500 mcg of folic acid administered through schools and Anganwadi centers.
Dietary strategies to combat pediatric anemia center on enhancing iron density and bioavailability.
